claim.text: The trajectory of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance, measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and related metrics, during supervised training decomposes into three distinct stages: (A) an initial stage where training and test error fall and AUROC improves; (B) a subsequent overfitting stage where the training error approaches zero and test error can continue to decrease while AUROC decreases; and (C) a final instability stage where classification test error is stable but AUROC varies sharply across nearby checkpoints, making final-checkpoint selection unreliable.
The instability of out-of-distribution (OOD) metrics near the final checkpoint arises from the trained solution being fragile to small perturbations of network weights.

Evaluating the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) as the weights are moved along random normalized directions \(d\) with small scalar magnitude \(\alpha\) (i.e., \(\theta(d,\alpha)=\theta_{\text{final}}+\alpha\cdot d\)) shows narrow optima in the weight space causing sharp metric changes for small \(\alpha\).
Applying exponential moving-weight averaging (Model Averaging, MA) stabilizes OOD performance by producing a smoother / wider optimum.

The averaged parameters \(\theta^{\mathrm{MA}}\), implemented as the exponential moving average of parameters after an epoch \(t_0\) (\(\theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MA}}=\theta_t\) for \(t<t_0\), and \(\theta_{t+1}^{\mathrm{MA}}=\tau\cdot \theta_t^{\mathrm{MA}} + (1-\tau)\cdot \theta_{t+1}\) for \(t\ge t_0\), with \(\tau=\dfrac{t-t_0}{t-t_0+1}\)), yield substantially reduced AUROC and FPR95 sensitivity to small weight perturbations and smoother AUROC curves during training across scoring functions.

For a simplified linear-Gaussian model that isolates a special discriminative feature and \(d\) abundant weak common features, the Bayes classifier and its in-distribution (ID) classification risk and out-of-distribution (OOD) detection (rejection) risk admit closed-form expressions.

The Bayes logit is \[ f_{\mathrm{Bayes}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = x_1 + \eta\sum_{i=2}^{d+1} x_i, \] and the resulting risks simplify to \[ \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ID}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}{\sigma}\right\}, \] \[ \mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{OOD}}(f_{\mathrm{Bayes}})=\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta-d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\}+\Pr\!\left\{\mathcal{N}(0,1)>\frac{\delta+d\eta^2}{\sigma\sqrt{1+d\eta^2}}\right\}, \] where \(\delta\) is the rejection threshold.
These formulas show that increasing the number \(d\) of common weak features (with \(0<\eta\ll1\) and \(d\gg1\)) can markedly increase OOD risk.
These formulas show that increasing the number \(d\) of common weak features (with \(0<\eta\ll1\) and \(d\gg1\)) only slowly improves ID classification.

Solving the squared-error empirical risk with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regularization parameter \(\lambda\), \[ \min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\ \mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_\text{ID}}\!\left\{\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\boldsymbol{w}^\top\boldsymbol{x}}{\sigma}-y\right)^2+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{w}\|_1\right\}, \] yields the closed-form trimmed coefficient vector \[ f_{\text{LASSO}}(\boldsymbol{x}) = (1-\lambda)_+\,x_1 + \sum_{i=2}^{d+1} (\eta-\lambda)_+\, x_i, \] where \((\cdot)_+\) denotes the positive part.
This analytic solution demonstrates that an \(L_1\) penalty can suppress coefficients on abundant weak common features (feature selection) (by choosing \(\lambda\approx\eta\)).
As a consequence of claim 11, this thereby reduces OOD detection risk at controlled cost to ID accuracy.
Pruning reduces learned common features, addressing overfitting.
Model averaging widens optima, addressing instability.
The combined module, Average of Pruning (AoP), which combines iterative magnitude pruning with parameter averaging, is applied without modifying existing scoring functions.
Applying Average of Pruning (AoP) as a plug-in improves out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance across multiple benchmarks and scoring methods.

On ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10, applying AoP to K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) increases average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) across six OOD datasets from 94.39% to 95.04% and reduces average false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) from 34.42% to 25.30%.

Applying AoP to Virtual-Logit Matching (ViM) on ResNet-18 trained on CIFAR-10 increases average AUROC from 94.18% to 95.69% and reduces average false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) from 32.27% to 25.3%.
AoP also improves multiple scoring functions.
AoP scales to larger datasets.
On Tiny-ImageNet, AoP improves MSP AUROC by 1.5–3.3 percentage points on Textures, LSUN, and iSUN.
On ImageNet, AoP yields AUROC improvements of 0.3–0.7 percentage points across scoring functions on Places, SUN, and Textures.
The improvements in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance achieved by applying Average of Pruning (AoP) as a plug-in hold across backbones.
The improvements in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance achieved by applying Average of Pruning (AoP) as a plug-in remain when combining AoP with Outlier Exposure (OE).
Iterative magnitude pruning (Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) style with weight rewinding) reduces the late-stage overfitting of out-of-distribution (OOD) detection.

As global sparsity is increased from dense toward moderate sparsity, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) on out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks first increases and then eventually decreases if pruning becomes too aggressive and removes discriminative capacity.
Visualization of final-layer features shows that pruned models produce larger ID-versus-OOD feature differences than dense models.
Different pruning schedules and methods matter.
LTH with weight rewind outperforms random pruning and naive fine-tuning based pruning in OOD metrics.
Among during-training pruning methods evaluated, iterative/post-training LTH performed best for OOD tasks in CIFAR-10 experiments with ResNet-18.
Ablation experiments establish that both components—model averaging (MA) and pruning—are required.
Pruning alone improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) relative to the dense baseline.
Combining pruning with MA (Average of Pruning, AoP) yields the best performance.
On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18: baseline AUROC = 91.63%; with pruning alone AUROC increases to 92.94%; with pruning plus MA (AoP) AUROC further increases to 93.32%.
Similar trends hold for WideResNet-28-10 and other metrics.
Pruning reduces overfitting.
MA stabilizes the weights/landscape for more reliable scoring.
Average of Pruning (AoP) not only improves out-of-distribution (OOD) detection but also enhances misclassification detection (detecting when the classifier will be wrong on in-distribution inputs).

On WideResNet-40-2 trained on CIFAR-10, applying AoP to Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for misclassification detection from 92.51% to 93.23%, reduces the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) from \(7.55\times 10^{-3}\) to \(6.41\times 10^{-3}\), and reduces the false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95) from 40.87% to 38.47%.
Similar improvements to those described in claim 38, claim 39 are observed when AoP is combined with other confidence estimators.
AoP also improves Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) and MaxLogit.

The improvements in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection performance achieved by applying Average of Pruning (AoP) as a plug-in hold across the ResNet variants, WideResNet, VGG, and MobileNet backbones.

Among the three during-training pruning methods evaluated—Gradual Magnitude Pruning (GMP), Rigging the Lottery (RigL), and Gradual Network with neuroregeneration (GraNet)—iterative/post-training LTH performed best for OOD tasks in CIFAR-10 experiments with ResNet-18.
Similar trends hold for WideResNet-28-10 and the other two metrics, area under the precision-recall curve (AUPR) and false positive rate at 95% true positive rate (FPR95).
Similar improvements to those described in claim 38, claim 39 are observed when AoP is combined with the other confidence estimator Confidence-aware Learning (CRL).
